utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-13/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic, and Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My name is Moore, I'm a Senior Trial Attorney. I appear today with Ms. Marie Tuma, Mr. Karim Khan Agha, Ms. Meritxell Regue, and Mr. Alex Demirdjian, and last but not least our case manager, Ms. Sandra D'Angelo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. For the defence of Mile Mrksic, Attorney Miroslav Vasic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. The defence of Miroslav Radic will be represented by Borivoje Borovic, attorney from Belgrade, and Mira Tapuskovic, also an attorney from Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the accused Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody here taking part in the proceedings. My name is Novak Lukic, Defence counsel for Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin and with me is co-counsel Momcilo Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Good morning. The city of Vukovar is an old and ancient city. It can trace its roots to the 14th Century. It has been described in a European guidebook from the 1950s as being located on the banks of the River Danube. It's considered to be pleasant, charming, picturesque, and attractive. A visit was recommended. On the 19th of November of 1991, a television crew from Britain made such a visit and this was what they found:

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: According to Ambassador Herbert Okun, who was the special envoy to the United Nations Secretary-General when he visited Vukovar on the 19th of November of that same year, he described it as follows: "Vukovar was the most destroyed city during the entire fighting in Croatia. Almost every building, every structure was destroyed or shot by shell-fire. Destruction was everywhere." We will hear from Ambassador Okun in due course. To the Serbs, Vukovar represented, as they saw it, a reincarnation of the Croatian tenancy towards duplicity and a drive towards independence. That had manifested itself previously with the fascist and Nazis in World War II. The pejorative word Ustasha was used by many to give vent to their feelings. With each rebuff of the Yugoslav army, repeated humiliation was heaped upon it, magnified undoubtedly by the veracious coverage of world's media. To the fledging Croat nation, the prolonged fighting in Vukovar by its troops against, as they saw it, overwhelming odds was a heroic beacon for Croats in their pursuit for freedom and independence. And consequently it is into this cauldron that the acts and deeds of individuals between the 18th and the 21st of November, 1991, specifically in Vukovar must be viewed and not through, as some would say, the rose-tinted spectacles of drawing-room reflections. This case concerns war crimes and crimes against humanity that were committed in the course of the attack on and shortly after the surrender of the city of Vukovar in November. The crimes charged in this indictment all relate to the detention, mistreatment and eventual killing of more than 260 Croat and non-Serb civilians taken from the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th and 20th of November. Many of those removed had been undergoing medical treatment prior to the removal and subsequent murder. And so consequently the events for which these accused stand trial were part after widespread and systematic attack against Croats and non-Serbs in the municipality of Vukovar. All the sequence of events which led to the mass grave at Ovcara form part of a well-organised and continuous line of action by those involved. The accused in this case, Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin, during the period of the indictment were serving officers in Belgrade or the Belgrade-based Guards Motorised Brigade, and hereafter I will call them the Guards. The criminal conduct of each of the accused by itself and with acts committed by others with whom they shared a common criminal purpose in our submission makes them criminally liable for the charges contained in the indictment under Article 7(1). Additionally, the failure of the accused to prevent or punish the criminal conduct of their subordinates makes them each liable for the charges contained under Article 7(3) of the Statute. May I just deal very briefly with the topic of military structure that we say will hopefully clarify several aspects of this case. The armed forces consisted of the Yugoslav People's Army, I'll call it JNA from now on if I may, and the Territorial Defence, also TO. The JNA was composed of a General Staff and three branches: Army, air force, and air defence and navy. There were three military districts, and the district which we are concerned with is the 1st Military District covering Western Serbia, the largest part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Eastern Croatia, including Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem where the city of Vukovar is situated at that particular location. In addition to the General Staff and the three branches, there is also a separate body in the armed forces that dealt with security matters, including counter-intelligence known as the security administration. Sljivancanin himself was the security officer of the Guards Motorised Brigade during the time and during the period relevant to this indictment, but as such he had no de jure commander responsibility. But due to the specific task or role consisting of the protection and security of the SFRY political and military leadership, the Guards Motorised Brigade was not part of the military district as such, rather - and importantly - it was directly subordinated to the SSNO, the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence. It was an elite unit within the JNA. It received the most capable officers and the most capable other ranks. They were, quite simply, the elite who guarded the elite. The brigade itself, which was under the command of then Colonel Mrksic, and during the period relevant for the indictment it consisted of two guard motorised battalions, two military police battalions which in our submission is important, one armoured battalion, a battalion for the protection of facilities and support elements. And the fact that it had not one but two military battalions, military police battalions, we say is important because it gave them a capacity. It gave them a capacity to protect and control situations more than most other brigades. This can, by comparison, be looked at or compared with a regular motorised JNA brigade which generally only had one company of military police. Let us move on to the Territorial Defence or the TO. Prior to the start of the armed conflict in Croatia, the police and the TO of the Republic of Croatia had split into Croatian and local Serb structures. In areas where local Serbs had a majority or significant minority, they took over the existing structures or set up their own police and TO units, and often staffs that did not answer to the republican authorities as they were perceived to be in Croatia. They stayed loyal to what remained of SFRY and Serbia. And so therefore, the process of creating a local Serb TO in Croatia started around about January 1991. Finally, may I deal with what are called volunteers. In 1982, the All People's Defence law was allowed. It was under well-defined legal circumstances. The purpose was to replenish the SFRY armed forces, the JNA and TO, with those same volunteers. They were people who were not subject to military service but who had been accepted in the armed forces. In view of their rights and responsibilities, volunteers were perceived as being on an equal footing with the military personnel or military conscripts. May I deal briefly now with what could be called, I suppose, command and control, and the Court will hear evidence principally from General Pringle in relation to that topic. With regard to the SFRY Presidency, that was the most senior command and control body in respect of the armed forces. However, unity of command, single authority were considered essential principles for the successful execution of military operations as indeed one finds in many armies throughout the world. A commander was typically assisted by a command staff who had to be able to provide him at any time during operations with detailed information about the situation. It was considered essential that a commander at all times should know the situation of his subordinate units two levels down. Orders were given quite clearly to maintain this system during the conflict in Croatia. Again, it is important to note that each SFRY armed forces officer was obliged to report violations of the laws of war. Officers bore liability for their actions, for the actions of their subordinates, and could be held personally responsible for a failure to prevent or punish crimes that occurred under their command. And we will see in due course an order that was sent to Mrksic, amongst others, from the superior, namely General Panic, that this principle had specific application, especially after the fall of Vukovar on the 18th of November. May I ask the Court, please, to just turn momentarily to what I will call a map folio. There are six maps which the Court can peruse in its own time. I have little doubt that that the Court is well aware of the various parts and locations. To assist, perhaps map 3 is the clearest where it delineates Croatia quite specifically, and we can see the River Danube flowing on the right-hand side, principally north/south, and we can see Vukovar on the Danube itself. Map 4 perhaps is an extension. And then if we go to map 6, there is a composite map created which shows Vukovar itself, and we have attempted to demonstrate and show where the important locations are, the hospital. A video will be shown of that in a moment; Velepromet was really a staging post to move on; Ovcara where the atrocities occurred; the barracks; and one of the headquarter areas, especially for the TO. So by the early 1990s the Republic of Croatia was clearly heading for independence. After a 19th of May referendum regarding its future in the Yugoslav federation, Croatia declared its independence on the 25th of June of 1991. The consequence was perfectly straightforward. Most Serbs living in Croatia did not participate in this referendum because they anticipated Croatia's independence. They had already held a referendum in late August and early September the previous year, and in that referendum, via the Serbian National Council, Serbs living in Croatia pronounced themselves in favour of a Serbian autonomy as a federal unit of the SFRY. And so consequently, regrettably ethnic identification became more apparent than had hitherto been the case. And in this context Croatian Serbs were being armed since 1990, attacks or we would submit that attacks on Croatian villages by JNA and Serb TO started in late spring, early summer 1991, for example, shelling of various towns. There was escalating tension between the two communities which clearly resulted in a general armed conflict approximately in August of 1991. Prior and during the armed conflict, villages were devastated. Croat civilians were abducted. They were tortured. They were raped. They were obliged to perform forced labour, and some of them were brutally killed by the JNA and Serb TOs. That was done on a systematic and sometimes indiscriminate basis. In addition, a large number of Croat civilians were forced to flee as Serb forces were taking control of their villages. Clearly the position of the JNA was paramount, and it was within that increasingly violent and the political context that the JNA was ostensibly, we would suggest, sent to Croatia to separate the conflicting parties and restore order between the Croatian authorities and as it was perceived to be the insurgent Croatian Serbs. However, it soon became clear that in reality at the latest from around the summer of 1991 onwards large parts of the JNA command and units in Croatia were supporting the insurgent Croatian Serbs in their armed struggle against the Croatian authorities. We submit that was done in order to consolidate Serb territorial gains, and by around September 1991, two months prior to the matters at Vukovar, units of the JNA 1st Motorised Division, acting in conjunction with the Serb TO units from SBWS and TO units from the Republic of Serbia and Serbian volunteers, had taken over most of the villages in Baranja, Eastern Slavonija, Western Srem, with the exception of Vukovar, and it is for that reason that Vukovar was so important, because Vukovar, as we know, is located on the Croatian side of the River Danube. That divided Croatia from Serbia, and Vukovar was then perceived to be the last Croatian stronghold in Eastern Slavonija. It was clearly of strategic importance for both parties, but it was of enormous symbolic importance for both Serb and Croat. So consequently, from around about July 1991, the Serb forces launched military attacks against the city of Vukovar and without any immediate effect. And so on the 29th of September, which we submit is an important date, an extremely important order was implemented. It was the Guards Motorised Brigade, or it related to the Guards Motorised Brigade prior to its redeployment to SBWS, being resubordinated to the 1st Military District. By so ordering, Lieutenant General Panic, who was commander of that military district, subsequently created two operational groups. One was Operational Group North, and the other was Operational Group South, OG North covered Baranja and the part of Eastern Slavonija north of the Vuka River. This case, however, deals principally with the activities and command structure of OG South. And it's important to note from this date until the 24th of November, OG South was responsible for the largest part of Eastern Slavonija located south of the Vuka River and, therefore, was heavily involved in the siege of Vukovar. It was also exclusively and we would say significantly responsible for the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital. At all times relevant to this indictment, Mrksic was commander of the Guards and he commanded OG South. And OG South, as I say, consisted of the Guards together with the detachment of the local Serb TO and other units of the TO of the Republic of Serbia and some smaller JNA units. OG South was responsible for the largest part of Eastern Slavonija located south of the Vuka River and, as I say, was heavily involved in the fighting around Vukovar. There was a functioning chain of command and a functioning reporting system between OG South command and its Commander Colonel Mrksic and its subordinate units. May we now turn, please, to Major Sljivancanin. He was chief of the security organs of the Guards, and he was clearly subordinate to Mrksic, and indeed it was Mrksic who later ordered Sljivancanin to organise and lead the evacuation of the hospital. Sljivancanin was the security officer of OG South, and as I've already said he consequently had no actual command responsibility according to JNA regulations. However, we submit that Sljivancanin's duties during the operations of OG South against Vukovar went beyond those of a regular security officer, and I will attempt to deal with those duties and subsequent actions or perhaps more appropriately inactions later on in this opening. And then finally, I want to deal with the third defendant, Captain Miroslav Radic. In the course of 1991, in October, Mrksic introduced what were called assault detachments. They were within OG South, and they were directly subordinated to him. Major Tesic was the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment and that played a major role in the siege of Vukovar. This particular detachment consisted of three assault groups with the accused, Captain Radic, as the commander of the 3rd Assault Group. And as I say, it's important to note that the component parts of this assault group and the individuals concerned. Radic's assault group was comprised of regular JNA, reservists, and Serb TO Vukovar detachments of which I will describe in due course. The Petrova Gora Detachment was commanded by a gentleman called Stanko Vujovic, and he is currently on trial in Belgrade for war crimes committed in Vukovar, with a man called Stanko Vujanovic, who also is currently on trial in Belgrade for war crimes committed in Vukovar, and he was believed to be his deputy. The Leva Supoderica TO Detachment was commanded by a person who was known as Kameni, and he was currently, as I say, on trial for war crimes committed at Vukovar. The command post for Radic's assault group was based at 81 Nova Ulica. And Your Honours may remember on map 6 that that is located on the diagram itself. And that was in the house of Vujanovic. During the siege of Vukovar, regular meetings were held at this command post to plan the military operations that were to be undertaken by Radic's assault group. These meetings were regularly attended by Vujovic, Vujanovic, and Kameni, as well as Major Sljivancanin, who curiously was considered by many of the Serb forces to be the commander of the whole Vukovar operation. But Radic was a close, or should I say that Radic had a close relationship with the Vukovar Serb TO detachments under his command as well as with Sljivancanin. According to one witness, Sljivancanin considered Radic as his right-hand man. And if I may put it in simplistic language, what I would submit and what we submit is that Radic basically was a conduit pipe between Sljivancanin and the local TO. On or about the 12th of November, 1991, the Serbian nationalist leader and head of the SRS and well known moderate Seselj, who is currently indicted and appearing at this particular Tribunal, visited Vukovar and held a meeting at Radic's command post. That was at the address at 81 Nova Ulica. In addition to Seselj, other persons, including the Guards Officers, were there, Sljivancanin, Radic, a man called Bojkovski, the Vukovar and local Serb TO commanders Vujovic, Vujanovic and Kameni who was also known to be politically affiliated with the SRS. Seselj was heard by a witness to be called to state to the participants who were at the meeting that, and I quote: "We are all one army. This war is a great test for Serbs. Those who pass the test will become winners. Deserters cannot go unpunished. Not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive." It is interesting to note that five years after the horrors of Vukovar that Sljivancanin stated in an interview with a newspaper that he agreed with Seselj's politics and also stated that he believed that Arkan was a brave man. Radic was clearly the most junior of the three defendants. Nevertheless, as I've already submitted, he played a crucial role. He was, as I say, the conduit pipe. He was in regular contact with the TO. Additionally, he was seen to be Sljivancanin's right-hand man and therefore carried the authority of Sljivancanin. Not only did he perform this important function of liaising with the local Serb TO but also by the use of the lists of people of which we will hear who were at the hospital at the fall of Vukovar, he was one of those who decided who went where. The meeting with Seselj and the observations made are important to the extent that it demonstrates a political partiality of those who attended, and it was only a mere six days before these atrocities occurred. The Prosecution submit that at this meeting a goal or intention to persecute all non-Serb opponents and Croats in Vukovar by members of what I will call the JCE may have started to take shape. During September and October of 1991, the forces of OG South, under the command of Mrksic, had almost completely surrounded and cut off the city of Vukovar. Throughout the approximately three-month period and the siege by the Serb forces the city, including the hospital, was subjected to a repeated, continuous, and often indiscriminate intense artillery and air bombardment campaign forcing many of its inhabitants to live in underground shelters or basements. As a part its operations to seize the city, the Serb forces also launched several infantry and armoured attacks, and so on the 18th of November, the Croatian forces defending Vukovar had finally surrendered. And during the course of that three-month siege, we have already seen from the introductory video that there was significant damage to the area and many people were killed and large numbers displaced. On or around the 18th of November, approximately 170 members of the Croatian forces who had been defending Vukovar surrendered in Mitnica. That was several kilometres from the city centre. During the negotiations for the surrender, the commanders of the Croatian forces surrendered to regular JNA units. However, these Croatian forces insisted that the surrender should be under the auspices of the Red Cross. This surrender also occurred in the full glare of the media, and two of those people involved were a gentleman called Colonel Pavkovic, again awaiting trial at ICTY but not in relation to this matter, but he was a liaison officer for OG South headquarters; and a gentleman called Nicolas Borsinger, who was from the International Committee of the Red Cross. Could I ask you, please, to turn to tab 4 and tab 5. May I deal with tab 5 first of all. So tab 5, please, and then we'll go back to tab 4 in a moment. Tab 5, I hope, will show for everybody individuals around a table. The gentleman on the left with the Red Cross badge is Nicolas Borsinger. We will see him in two days' time on the bridge in Vukovar. But we have Borsinger. The next gentleman to him is Pavkovic. We also will see him on the bridge. And the gentleman on the right is a person who is surrendering on behalf of the Croatian forces. Could I ask you now, please, to go to tab -- tab 4. I'm not going to play the video, that will come in due course, but I have a copy of a transcript, and I would like to deal with it in the following way, and I have highlighted for all parties what we would say are the salient parts. If we go to page 1, we can see that Pavkovic is saying, "Surrender, surrender." From if we then go to page 5, we see Pavkovic talking to a gentleman called Karaula who is a Croatian Defender. Pavkovic said, "You are the gentleman from Mitnica." And the answer is, "Yes." Six, Nicolas Borsinger comes in and what he says is important. He said, "I need to explain to both representatives the presence of the International Committee of the Red Cross here is only in relations with questions of humanitarian nature." And then on page 7, the part that I would ask the Court perhaps to underline, although it's already done, we can see Pavkovic giving the reason why the International Red Cross is actively involved. He says, "Members of the armed Croatian forces asked for a member of the International Red Cross or the monitoring mission to participate." He carries on, "Because that is, according to them, a guarantee that our agreement will be respected." We submit that this particular negotiation at Mitnica, which carried on and to be properly dealt with highlights quite specifically the concern of Croatian forces and the nature of the surrender. It is also important in relation to Pavkovic's state of knowledge and Borsinger's participation on the bridge at Vukovar. And so as a consequence, the Croatian forces who had surrendered on this occasion were escorted by the Guards military police without any interference from the local Serb TO. They were taken to the border with Serbia and after which they were transported to the detention camp in Serbia. It may well be that the involvement of the Red Cross itself, and in particular the presence, initially, that that may well have saved the lives of those surrendering. If the presence of the International Red Cross and the media was a miscalculation, it was not a miscalculation that was to be repeated on the 20th of November and the evacuation from the hospital. During the last days of the siege at Vukovar, several hundred people converged, not surprisingly, on the hospital. They believed that it would be a safe place and a place to take refuge. By the 18th of November, those on the hospital premises, including medical staff, relatives of staff, patients, including people who had been injured during the fighting of other civilians were located. Many at the hospital stayed in the basement on account of the JNA shelling of the hospital, which had already caused extensive damage to the upper floors of the hospital itself. It is estimated by the 18th of November there were approximately between 1 and 2.000 people taking -- people taking refuge in the hospital in addition to the sick and injured. And I would like to play, if I may, please, a short video that was taken at the time of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Around the time of the surrender of the forces defending Vukovar, an evacuation agreement was signed in Zagreb. It was signed by the representatives of the Republic of Croatia, the JNA, the International Committee of the Red Cross, Medicins Sans Frontieres, and the Malteser Kreuz. The evacuation agreement was clearly an important document and was designed to regulate the evacuation of the sick and the wounded from the hospital under the auspices of the monitors themselves. Would the Court please refer to the binder and go to tab 1, and we will activate it on Sanction. May we deal with the first paragraph which I hope is highlighted. One can see that there is a meeting on the 18th of November. If we move to paragraph 5, "The evacuation will include all those wounded or sick undergoing medical treatment in the Vukovar Hospital ..." Paragraph 6: "The hospital will be put under the protection of the International Red Cross who will advise both parties of the period for neutrality which they require." And then 7: "The Republic of Croatia and the YPA agree that the European Commission Monitor Mission should monitor the whole of the operation having full access to all elements of the evacuation." And then there's reference to facilitation. And we submit that the reference to "all the wounded and sick," that quite simply it was to be under the protection of the International Red Cross literally from beginning to end, and the monitoring was more honoured in the breach than anything else. No mention was made whatsoever in the evacuation agreement of the JNA handing over the evacuees to any other body. Indeed, there was no mention made in the agreement about the role to be played by the self-declared local SBWS authorities in the evacuation of the hospital. The evacuation agreement was known to all parties. It was known by these three defendants and others, and there were many other elements that came into play that to some extent actually strengthened the agreement rather than weakened it. The fighting between the Serb forces and the Croatian forces had been very intense. There clearly had been high losses for both sides, in particular the Serb forces. The Guards itself had suffered particularly heavy losses, especially amongst officers. Colonel Mrksic apparently observed that they, namely the Guards, had more than 600 men put out of action, including many officers, and this would probably be recorded in the history of war as a military operation in which more officers were killed than soldiers. It puts really in mind the word "decimate," which means one in ten, in Latin and here. There was approximately 600 men who were either killed or injured out of a total of approximately 3.000. Anticipating the strong possibility of reprisals against the civilian population of Vukovar after its fall, General Panic issued an order to Colonel Mrksic to seize the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th of November. This order, we submit, is an extremely important document in the case. It unambiguously put Mrksic on notice concerning the threat of retribution and other sorts of revenge for which some local Serb TO units had been responsible. May I just ask you, please, to turn to tab 2. If we go to Sanction for that. If we deal with the first page, we can see in the top left-hand corner, which is one -- or the 1st Military District, which clearly is here. The 18th of November is the date. We can see that it is highlighted as being very urgent. It relates to Operations Group South under the control and command of Mrksic. If I then turn the page, we can see in paragraph 3: "While carrying out these assignments, and in all other operations in the area, which the 1st Military District are engaged on smashing Ustasha forces, observe all aspects of the Geneva Convention on the prisoners of war." May we go on, please, to paragraph 8: "Every unit must fully control the situation on the territory of its area of responsibility." And again: "Commanders at all levels will be responsible for this. Wartime laws have not entered into force and therefore - as always - nobody has the right to retribution and other kinds of revenge, which some local TO /Territorial Defence/ units carried out. In future, arrest those who commit any such acts and undertake appropriate legal measures." At the very bottom we can see where it is originating from. It's in Mrksic's superior, Panic. And then finally, if we go to the last page, we can see it is the 18th of November at 0045 hours when it was received. And we would submit that, if I may use the English phrase, it is as plain as a pikestaff to anyone receiving that order exactly what Panic was concerned about. Over and above just a question of common sense of what had been occurring for two months previously. Dr. Bosanac, who will be our first witness, was the director of the hospital. She had been informed that the evacuation of the sick and wounded from the hospital would start on the 18th of November under, as has been arranged, the auspices of the Red Cross and the European Monitors. The evacuation, however, could not take place on that day because both groups were involved in monitoring the surrender and evacuation of civilians in other parts of the city, almost certainly Mitnica as I have already referred. Therefore, it is agreed that the monitors would instead go to the hospital to monitor its evacuation the next day, namely the 19th of November. During the evening of the 18th of November, because Mrksic seems to have had a command briefing each day, but on the evening of the 18th of November, Mrksic held, as I would submit, his customary daily command briefing at the headquarters at Negoslavci. There he announced that Sljivancanin would be in command of the operation to evacuate the hospital. And so on the morning of the 19th of November, Major Tesic and his forces of the 1st Assault Detachment reached the hospital and secured it. There was no resistance from anybody in the hospital. And at approximately the same time Radic also reached the hospital. You will remember, of course, that Radic was directly subordinated to Tesic but curiously had not been ordered by Tesic to go to the hospital or to take any part in the evacuation. It would appear that Radic himself attended the hospital of his own volition, and it is correct to say that Sljivancanin then joined Radic. Shortly after Tesic's arrival at the hospital, Vujic -- I beg your pardon, Vujovic, Vujanovic and other members of the local Serb Vukovar TO, including Serb volunteers and paramilitaries, started gathering outside the hospital. Bearing in mind that the order had been given by Panic the day before, these individuals were allowed entry despite, we would submit, the obvious dangers in such a potentially highly charged environment. Some of these people identified themselves as Chetniks, and as I say, they were allowed to enter by the JNA. And there they started abusing, they started beating and otherwise mistreating some of the patients. While feelings were clearly running high within the local Serb TO, this was the real first manifestation of actual incidents occurring within the JNA, and we submit there was complicity here in respect of that, bearing in mind that it was perfectly foreseeable trouble would occur when the battles had occurred sometime previously Not surprisingly, Bosanac insisted that the monitors themselves should be present when the evacuation occurred, perfectly in line with the evacuation agreement, and she endeavoured to contact the monitor to this effect. When she was talking to Major Sljivancanin concerning access to the hospital, the -- regarding Dr. Bosanac's prudent request, the European Monitor Schou received a rely from Sljivancanin that the European Monitors should have no further contact with her because Sljivancanin considered her to be a criminal and that they should not be allowed to go to the hospital while there were criminals present Tesic then took Bosanac back to the OG South headquarters to meet with Mrksic, and at that meeting Mrksic informed Bosanac that he was changing the evacuation route that had been agreed upon. Apparently there was a concern expressed about mines. Mrksic also informed Bosanac that the Red Cross was busy at the Velepromet facility in Vukovar dealing with the since that were gathered there and Mrksic also added that Bosanac should return to the hospital and await the International Red Cross monitors there. Curiously, he refused to allow Bosanac to speak to one of the monitors at the headquarters using the phrase, "Well, there was no reason for her to see them now." So Bosanac was quite simply taken back to the hospital, and it was quite clear that the military police were in complete control at that time. Around that day, it was the 19th of November, Ambassador Okun and Cyrus Vance were there. They were the international peace envoys in relation to a mission in respect of the International Conference for the former Yugoslavia. They also attempted to visit the hospital in order to assess the situation there, but we will hear evidence from Okun in this trial about what occurred. After her return to the hospital, Dr. Bosanac discovered that the JNA, under Sljivancanin, had actually already started separating the men from the women and transporting them to the collection facility at Velepromet, and this was done clearly in breach of the agreement and clearly with no adherence whatsoever of what had been intended. Despite her protests to Sljivancanin that this should not be done without the monitors being present, Sljivancanin completely disregarded her and continued separating and selecting the evacuees from the hospital complex. As I say, this was men and women being separated. And so consequently by the late afternoon or early evening on the 19th of November, under Sljivancanin's order, a large number of the people who had previously sought refuge at the hospital had been transported to the collection centre at Velepromet, which was clearly under the JNA control Many of these people were subsequently mistreated. Some were killed at the facility, and some of that facility was being used as a detention centre. Sometime after the earlier evacuation of the civilians to Velepromet, a representative of the Red Cross arrived at the hospital and met with Bosanac and Sljivancanin. What then occurred, we submit, was highly significant, because in actual fact Bosanac gave a list of sick and wounded to the international representative. The reason is perfectly obvious. The evacuation agreement specified about all those injured being under the control of the International Red Cross and other considerations as well. Sljivancanin, however, requested copies of the list of the sick and wounded, and bearing in mind the pressure that was being applied and the situation, Bosanac reluctantly gave copies to him. Again, on his insistence and despite her reluctance, Bosanac arranged for other lists to be made of the hospital staff, family members, and other persons in the hospital to be given to Sljivancanin. We suggest, or we submit, that Sljivancanin himself was clearly taking control of the lists to serve his own end. Those same lists, we submit, were later used for selection purposes in the evacuation of the hospital. And so when we come to the evening of the 19th of November, Mrksic held a meeting at his head quarter quarters and he informed a number officers who had been sent to assist in the evacuation of Vukovar Mrksic uttered the following words: "Many criminals are hiding amongst the wounded who have been killing and slaughtering the JNA soldiers and Serb civilians." Later that same evening, Bosanac again was taken back to Mrksic's headquarters. However, Sljivancanin was there, and he started questioning her about the whereabouts of, as he said, various members of the Croatian forces defending Vukovar. And so as I have already said, you have Bosanac at the headquarters and a number of people at Velepromet. The facility itself held a large number of individuals who had sought refuge previously or that they had been bused in the orders of Sljivancanin. The facility itself is located close to the JNA barracks in Vukovar and again was under the control of the OG South. A retired JNA security officer, a man called Colonel Vujic, was ordered to go to Velepromet and to separate, as was called, the prisoners of war from the civilians. Vujic was also to arrange for the prisoners of war to be bused to the detention facility at Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia. But when he arrived at Velepromet, he was introduced to a security officer in the Guards. That officer was in charge of the facility at Velepromet, and informed Vujic that the separation of prisoners of war and civilians again had already been completed, and more importantly, indicated that members of the local Serb TO were also assisting in the security of the facility. While inspecting the premises, Vujic was denied entry to one particular room. That was guarded by both members of the local Serb TO and the military police of the Guards Motorised Brigade. This room became known by those who either were held in it or aware of its function as the "Room of death." Two men, one of whom was referred as Topola and a gentleman called Marko Crevar were present. Both were known locally as Chetniks. Crevar, who was head of the secretariat of internal affairs in Vukovar and a part of the security detail at the facility was under the command -- under the command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, told Vujic the following: "They will not allow the POWs in the room to be taken out of it, but instead they will keep them in order to punish them, that is, deal with them the way they dealt with Serbs ... These are all criminals. We know they were personally. We are already dealing with them, and nobody will be able to take them away from us, even if we have to settle our accounts with weapons." However, Vujic, to his credit, noticed that people were being removed from the room. They were being taken away and after that shots were being heard. And as was later discovered, dead bodies were seen at the Velepromet facilities. At this point, Vujic himself ordered the crew of a Guards Motorised Brigade armoured personnel carrier to move their vehicle as close to the room as possible and to open fire on those guarding the room, including himself, if the prisoners held in that room were not released. On this threat of force, the members of the local Serb TO backed down and released the prisoners. It really begs the question, does it not, if Vujic was able to protect people, does it not beg the question how others were not able to do so later on? According to Vujic himself, he said that around 45 prisoners of war were taken out of that room. He described them as all being in a bad state, described them as bloody, beaten up, and generally looked bad. It was obvious that they had been tortured. There are other descriptions from that room. If I just give one by a man called Josip Covic, he said that: "Drunken Chetniks would arrive at night and pick out the young, stronger male prisoners. They would take them to the corner where they would be beaten to death in front of us. They would beat them with electric cables until they fell down, and when they were on the floor they would jump on them with their boots and kick them in the heads. While doing this, the Chetniks shouted, Squash them, kill the Ustasha, the motherfucker is still alive." Returning to the headquarters of OG South in the early hours of the 20th of November - and the day is significant - Vujic informed Mrksic in clear and unequivocal language and also Major Sljivancanin about the troubles that he had encountered with members of the local Serb TO, including the volunteers identifying themselves as Chetniks, what had occurred at Velepromet and that they were also killing certain non-Serb detainees. It appears that despite the warning from Panic, despite the warning from Vujic, that nothing was done by officers to protect those people. If Vujic is to be believed, he gives a clear and unequivocal account to both Mrksic and Sljivancanin of a clear course of conduct of extreme violence, killing of persons in their charge, and it is important obviously for two reasons: The account given by him is directly to both Mrksic and Sljivancanin and from a highly credible and reliable source; and secondly, it reconfirms the fears expressed to Mrksic and Sljivancanin from their commander Panic in the order of the 18th of November, some 36 hours earlier. And the fears that Panic had expressed clearly were now coming to fruition. Indeed, despite this information, Sljivancanin's attitude was somewhat interesting because he subsequently briefed Vujic and others that he had outsmarted Bosanac, that he had been able to acquire the lists of those who were at the hospital and, as I say, these lists, according to Sljivancanin, had revealed disguised war criminals in the hospital who were known to have committed crimes against the local Serb population. It is clear from the language used of "war criminals," that both he and Mrksic were ad idem with regard to their perception of many of the evacuees. We submit that the plan of Mrksic, Sljivancanin, Radic, and others involved in the evacuation of this hospital was to identify and to isolate the individuals whom they believed had committed crimes against the local Serb population and Serb forces, namely, they were war criminals or they were Ustashas. May I respectfully ask the Court if there could be a short adjournment at this time, and I will then continue with what I will call the second part of my submission.
