utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you, My Lord. May I just move on, please, to the evacuation of further individuals from the hospital itself. As I already indicated, Dr. Bosanac was taken back and forward to the hospital on several occasions. At approximately 6.00 in the morning on the 20th, Major Sljivancanin gave a briefing to Colonel Vujic and other officers before he travelled to -- travelled from the Velepromet facilities to the hospital itself. He stated that he himself would be personally in charge of evacuating the hospital, that his officers had already received their assignments, and that the people in the hospital would be gathered in the hospital yard where it would be decided who would be taken where. Clearly, we submit, the lists play an important function with regard to that. On account of the problems at Velepromet the night before, the selected individuals who would be taken from the hospital were to be evacuated to the JNA barracks, that was in Vukovar, and they clearly -- and was clearly before -- beside the Velepromet facility. This apparently was for the protection of those individuals. If it was for their own protection and it was a genuine explanation, then, we submit, it would clearly beg a question or questions: Protection from whom? And how did so many souls die in such dreadful circumstances approximately 12 hours later if indeed it was Sljivancanin's intention to protect them? On arrival at the hospital itself, the Guards personnel and the local Serb TO were all under Sljivancanin's command, as we submit, and they were still in control of the security at that time. Radic himself had also arrived at the hospital in the early morning. He met with Sljivancanin again, and Sljivancanin had been walking around and continued to walk around the hospital with members of the local Serb TO who identified and were identified as Chetniks, and what they were doing was they were pointing out Croats in the hospital and indicating ones that had slaughtered Serbs. All of this was being done in Sljivancanin's presence and with his collusion. With regard to that selection procedure and the involvement of the TO, bearing in mind what Vujic had seen and reported the night before, one can draw, we would submit, a perfectly reasonable and proper inference that what was being done here and the selection of these individuals was approved of by Sljivancanin. At around about 7.00, one hour later, Sljivancanin then informed Dr. Bosanac that she was no longer in charge of the hospital, and he told her that he was calling a meeting of the staff. She asked for a delay in the evacuation, clearly in adherence of the evacuation agreement she wanted the monitors to be there, and they were to be there at approximately 8.00. No delay was permitted. No delay was granted by Sljivancanin, and reluctantly Bosanac agreed for the meeting to be called. The reason, we submit, why there was no international monitors was perfectly straightforward. They were being deliberately delayed in getting to the hospital by the JNA, and we will hear evidence, I trust, that they were held for approximately two hours during which the evacuation of the hospital continued. The evacuation, but perhaps more importantly the selection of individuals which continued unfettered by the restriction that would be placed on it by the international eye and the media in particular. As I say, Mitnica was not going to be repeated. While the hospital staff meeting was in progress, a JNA officer read out from the lists of names those in the hospital who should go to the hospital yard. A selection procedure was clearly under way. And while this separation was taking place, some of the local Serb TOs and other paramilitaries had actually entered the hospital, again past the OG South security personnel and were continuing, as they had done the day before, threatening patients. It's also important to bear in mind what had happened the night before at Velepromet Sljivancanin was told about. And again it begs the question: How is it that the very category of individual who had been partially responsible for the cruelties and killings the night before were being allowed in the hospital that morning, because the personnel in the area did not intervene to protect these patients. One witness remembers the following: "I saw Chetniks hitting a man on the part of his leg that had been amputated." That was after he had been identified as a Croat. And when the separation was taking place, Sljivancanin himself was announcing to the hospital staff that the JNA had won the day and that the hospital was now under JNA control. No ICRC, no Red Cross representative or European Monitor was present in the hospital while this separation and removal was taking place, despite it being perfectly obvious that it was agreed that they should participate in that particular capacity. As I say, that was because they were being deliberately denied to the hospital by Sljivancanin and others. Furthermore, we suggest that the meeting was a ruse to distract into one place the only other group of people who could cause difficulties or delays in this targeted selection. Once the evacuees were in the yard of the hospital they were then put on buses. Sljivancanin again was directly responsible or in charge, should I say, of the operation. But it's important to note that his right-hand man Radic was fully involved at this time in the selection procedure and despite not being a military policeman or a member of the security personnel, and apparently in the absence of any order from his superior Tesic. The people who were being isolated, the people who were being targeted were principally military opponents, politicians from the Croatian Democratic Union, or perceived Croatian sympathisers. They were separated from the other evacuees, and as I say, loaded onto buses. Radic himself ordered some of the selected hospital evacuees onto the buses, and what was said, if I may give a small example of what was occurring, prior to the boarding of the buses evacuees were being searched. Perhaps that is understandable in its own way, but I quote: "I saw them take out Martin Dosen, who was one of those wounded from the hospital. Although he was on a stretcher, he was nevertheless pushed and just dumped in the courtyard to die." He is among those listed as missing and, indeed, in due course you will see that to be the case. "I saw many local Chetniks with the JNA, and they were beating the men," all in the courtyard, or in the forecourt, all clearly under the control of OG South. Sljivancanin was, according to one witness, well aware of the fate of the selected persons on the buses. According to one woman, when she spoke to Sljivancanin about the people on the buses, he replied to her that the detainees would not be going far because, and I quote: "They would be swallowed by the dark in the middle of the day." On an earlier visit to the hospital while looking at the wounded civilians being carried out to the hospital and in the presence of a journalist, Radic state that: "They (the wounded civilians) are all dead men." And when in actual fact the journalist queried that, the reply was: "You are not seeing clearly, these are dead men." Another OG South soldier assisted in the loading of the buses took money off evacuees. One in particular, a woman called Markobasic, was a well-known member -- or the wife of a well-known member of the Croatian forces who had defended Vukovar. She was told that she would have no use for any of the money. She was visibly pregnant at the time. She is one of the victims murdered in the most appalling of ways at Ovcara. A high-velocity weapon was inserted into her vagina and then fired, killing her as well as the unborn baby. The buses then proceeded from the hospital to the JNA barracks, and that was clearly at Vukovar, and each bus was accompanied by two military police and a Guards officer. All the buses bound for the barracks had departed from the hospital before Sljivancanin allowed the monitors from the European Commission and the International Red Cross to have access, and it is the significance of the timing and the release into the area that perhaps is indicative of the state of mind existing at that time. Simultaneously, while the selective separation of the evacuees and the loading of the buses were taking place at the hospital, the monitors, who had earlier left the headquarters of the JNA, were prevented, as I say, from entering or proceeding to the hospital. The place that they were delayed was at a bridge over the Vuka River, and that they seem to think was around about 8.45 in the morning. The reason given by Sljivancanin to them at that time was that they were being prevented from proceed together hospital for their own safety. You may hear Bosanac actually say that as she thought it was rather surprising some of the JNA soldiers were actually discharging weapons at that time, and we would submit it was almost certainly a ploy to give that impression. We submit that the stopping of the monitors from reaching the hospital and attempting to prevent Mr. -- or should I say Sljivancanin from removing the selected individuals was clearly in breach of the evacuation agreement, and it was only after the selected evacuees had been removed from the hospital that that was done. The monitors themselves estimated that they had been delayed for a period of approximately two years -- two hours. My apologies. Two hours. So equally, we would submit, if one thinks back to the 18th of November and the man called Pavkovic and Borsinger being present of the -- or at the evacuation and surrender at Mitnica, and with regard to that here we can see quite simply that there was a deliberate ploy to delay. One representative of the European Commission says: "I saw that there was an armoured personnel carrier blocking the bridge. We were kept there for two hours. It struck me as nonsense because there was no longer any fighting. We were arguing with Sljivancanin in the strongest possible way, so that we would be allowed into the hospital. During that time, a Red Cross representative arrived and got into a strong argument with Sljivancanin in front of the bridge. Sljivancanin turned to me and told me that he did not trust the Red Cross ..." As I say, at the same time that the monitors were being deliberately delayed, there was traffic moving freely on a parallel bridge over the Vuka River, which had been, as it were, released for traffic. The purpose, however, was perfectly clear. One had to get across the river and across the bridge with those evacuees, and it had been recently open, we submit, to permit the transfer of the detainees from the hospital to the barracks. Could I now, please, would the Court's leave show two things. One, I wish to show the video of what occurred on the bridge with Borsinger. That could be shown, and the transcript is at tab 6. However, what is being done also, if it helps, is that there are subtitles underneath in relation to the translation, and then draw attention to the photograph itself. So this is the confrontation with Borsinger who had been at Mitnica on the 18th, and here he is with Sljivancanin and Pavkovic that morning. Yes, please. Your Honours, I think, need to put on headsets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just deal with the transcript for one moment, at tab 6. You may have heard Sljivancanin said, "I gave you everything you asked for." That's at the bottom of page 3 of 3. In actual fact, Sljivancanin gave him absolutely nothing. The whole point was they didn't let the representative, Borsinger, go across the bridge at all. May I ask you, please, to turn to tab 10. This is a -- clearly what I will call a split photograph. We have just seen the confrontation on the bridge with Borsinger who had come after the earlier disagreements. One can see Borsinger on the right, Sljivancanin, on the left, and the gentleman in the middle is Pavkovic, and we can see, if we look at the photograph of two days earlier, that you have Borsinger on the left, and you've got Pavkovic in the middle. The other matter which you might wish to consider, entirely a matter for the Court, is there is an APC in behind, and one can see actually Pavkovic walk from the general direction of it. When we look at the video in due course, I will be highlighting that fact. And then we would submit that it's not without significant with the press there that suddenly that APC is started up and removed out of the way. And so in conclusion, here we have a gentleman, Pavkovic, who knew perfectly well what had gone on. He could authenticate what Borsinger was saying, and quite simply we would submit that these individuals were really deliberately delaying the arrival of the monitors in clear breach of that agreement. At the JNA barracks themselves, the buses with the evacuees there remained at the barracks for several hours still under the control of JNA OG South control, and throughout that time they were prevented from actually leaving the buses. It was almost as if they were a prison in themselves. However, despite the problems the night before, the warnings given by the colonel, by the commanding officer, and just common sense, the local Serb TO members, including the paramilitaries and the volunteers, they were allowed to enter the barracks and also to threaten the evacuees in the buses. They stated quite openly they were going to settle scores with the evacuees. One was told that in actual fact that he would not be saved and he would face a bad end. At the barracks, the selection procedure continued. Some of the occupants on the buses were released. Those who were released were released because they were identified as relatives of hospital staff or listed as being erroneously placed on the bus. It is the purpose of the list that we submit is important. Some evacuees were saved by neighbours and friends. Many of those released were beaten actually in front of JNA OG South soldiers, and then they were returned to the hospital. One witness remembers: "Twenty-five people being taken off the buss in total ... As we were taken off, we had to go through a line of Chetniks. They were all kicked and beaten with sticks and metal bars. The beating continued on the bus where there were three men, two were Chetniks and one was a young JNA regular." At one point Radic again became involved. He enter at least one of the buses at the JNA barracks and he read from a list of names of some of the occupants who were subsequently allowed off the bus. Quaere: Why are people being kept on the bus and what was intended for them? Because while at the barracks, both Vujovic and Vujanovic, who were the leaders of the local TO, were present, and they also had discussions was Sljivancanin. In the early hours of the afternoon, those buses carrying the evacuees from the hospital left the JNA barracks under the JNA OG South escort, and they were bound for Ovcara and, we submit, on the orders of Mrksic through Sljivancanin. Simultaneously, a large pit or grave requiring the use of a mechanical digger, the pit was being dug nearby at Ovcara. It was under the control of a JNA soldier. At the same time, the detainees were being held at the barracks. A local man was used to start the digging. The ground had to be selected, and it was clearly so large it had to hold a number of bodies. Two hundred bodies were found in that grave. And the significance is obvious. It was clearly and does clearly demonstrate that there was an intention to kill, to bury, and to hide. And the size of the grave is significant, because it suggests a premeditation with regard to numbers. In actual fact, some 60 people are still unaccounted for, such has been the ability to hide. The whole procedure, we submit, suggests organisation of military precision, both with regard to transportation and timing where the evacuees are under the control of OG South and under the control of Mrksic. Can I ask the Court, please, to just bear in mind the statements of Sljivancanin and Radic the previous day. Radic: "They are all dead men." And Sljivancanin: "They would be swallowed by the dark in the middle of the day." We submit that the threatening and aggressive conduct of the local Serb TO towards the evacuees on the buses prior to their removal to Ovcara, it was open, it was visible to the officers of the Guards, it was visible and obviously known to Sljivancanin who additionally had been aware of the fate of the Velepromet detainees the night before, yet nothing was done to rectify the situation. Why not, if the actual and genuine intention was to protect as had been declared? Around this same time there was additionally a meeting of the self-declared SBWS government under Hadzic, currently indicted here. At this meeting was discussed that although the evacuees removed from the hospital should be tried for any war crimes which they had committed, they should remain under the control of the JNA since civilian authority had not been properly established in Vukovar, and indeed why would it, bearing in mind that there had been war raging for something like three months. Sljivancanin allegedly informed the meeting that military authority remained and that civil authority would not be established until further notice. Additionally, he informed the meeting that he would tell them when it would be possible to establish civil authority. Dealing with Ovcara for a moment. At least two scheduled and successful evacuations had taken place through Ovcara prior to the hospital evacuees' arrival via the JNA barracks. Those previous evacuations had taken place with the assistance of the 80th Motorised Brigade and that was under the orders of OG South. The 80th Brigade was a reserve brigade that had arrived in the area approximately the 7th of November of that year, but it was subordinated to OG South until the departure of the Guards from Vukovar on the 24th of November. The 80th was commanded by a gentleman called Lieutenant Colonel Milorad Vojnovic. They had their own security organ, but they had one military police company, and they had assisted in the earlier evacuations from Ovcara between the 19th and the 20th of November. Surprisingly, unlike on previous occasions, the 80th did not receive any notification or orders to assist in any further evacuation from Ovcara on the 20th. Vojnovic actually only became aware of the buses carrying the evacuees from the hospital when he passed by the hangar in order to inspect one of his detachments or units. So it was entirely coincidental that he became aware of it. We submit that the failure of OG South to notify the 80th of the arrival of the evacuees as it had been done on previous occasions is another indication that the evacuees sent here to Ovcara was for clearly another purpose as opposed to the transfer to Sremska Mitrovica in Serbia. The buses containing those hospital evacuees reached Ovcara sometime in the afternoon. They were escorted by military police. At this time, armed members of the local Serb TO also arrived at Ovcara. They quite literally had been following these individuals like a pack after a wounded animal. While the evacuees made their way from the buses to the hangar at Ovcara they were made to run through a gauntlet, as I would describe it, they were forced to run between two lines of soldiers. That included JNA, local Serb TO, and Serbian volunteers/paramilitaries. They were verbally abused, and they were severely beaten with rifle butts, metal bars and other objects. Sljivancanin was present when the evacuees were made to run the gauntlet. One witness described it as follows: "We had to run through a cordon of approximately 100 local Serbs, Chetniks and Serbian police who beat us with sticks, clubs, and canes. Whoever fell down never stood up again as they were beaten to death. All these men were holding weapons of some sort, like rifles, iron bars, large pieces of wood. They used these weapons to beat the bus passengers as they made their way towards the building." And after the buses were unloaded there were approximately 300 people in the hangar, some of whom were isolated behind a rope, and again here another list was made. Once inside the hanger, some of the evacuees were subject to further abuse and further beatings by the local Serb TO, paramilitaries, volunteers, and JNA OG South soldiers. And there is much description about what occurred. Again: "A little later four Chetniks came in with iron bars and gave us the most beating of all. That was followed by an elderly reservist coming in and blowing a whistle, which caused those Chetniks to go out and another four or five to come in and continue the beatings. The whistle was blown about every 20 minutes, and this lasted for about two hours." Those beatings were so severe that at least two of the evacuees were literally beaten to death. Many of the evacuees had been taken from the hospital in an injured state. Many others sustained serious injuries as a result of the beating in the hangar. Nevertheless, no medical treatment was offered to any of the detainees actually from the time of their transfer from the hospital throughout their stay at the JNA barracks and the hangar at Ovcara until their ultimate execution. Another description was: "I saw (Bulic) beat a man," and then gave the name "... with a baseball bat, and afterwards I could see no sign of life. I think he literally beat him to death. "The beating of Ekrem was so bad that I am convinced he died from his injuries. I saw them kicking him, beating him with weapons and stamping on his head and his body. They made him sing Chetniks songs. They beat and totally humiliated him until the time was that he looked dead." And as I've already said, one woman was shot through her vagina, killing herself and the child. During this mistreatment of the evacuees in the hangar attempts were made by some recently arrived members of the 80th Motorised Brigade to investigate the situation and attempt to restore order and stop the beatings. Officers from the Guards Motorised Brigade were present and in the hangar. Unfortunately, the officers of the 80th, assuming that the Guards were in charge of the evacuees at the hangar because they had not been notified of the procedure, did nothing at that time. And they assumed that in actual fact the guards were responsible for the prisoners. After order, however, was restored in the hangar, that was approximately the afternoon and early evening of the 20th, the military police of the 80th headed by a man called Vezmarovic apparently tried to protect the evacuees from the local Serbs. This again is another example of people trying to protect. Several evacuees were released and allowed to return to Vukovar at the time. They were released because they were either -- Serb friends or neighbours intervened or due to the fact that the detainee claimed to be a member of the JNA. Later in the evening, the commander of the military police company of the 80th Motorised Brigade, however, was ordered by a security officer of the Guards and a direct subordinate of Major Sljivancanin to withdraw from his unit from Ovcara and hand over the evacuees to the members of the local TO and the Serbian paramilitaries and volunteers. These were the same local TO that I've already mentioned on many occasions, paramilitaries that had congregated at Velepromet and at the hangar and were the same men who were responsible for the earlier threats and the beatings of the evacuees. And we submit that as planned, by the accused and other members, the JCE named in the indictment, some known and some not known, the evacuees were now to be executed by the local TO, including volunteers and paramilitaries. And throughout this whole time there was the command and control exercised by Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic and others. Shortly after the JNA OG South officers handed over the evacuees to the local TO, the evacuees were then subdivided into groups of 10 and 20. They were then loaded group by group onto a truck/trailer, and because of the number involved that was obliged to make several return trips so that the evacuees could all be transported to a ravine close to the hangar at Ovcara. At the ravine, the detainees were all executed, truckload by truckload, by the local Serb TO as well as volunteers and by members of the JNA who formed part of OG South. The period of execution lasted from the late afternoon and throughout the night. Shots were heard during the night by some members of the 80th, despite the apparent efforts by the executioners, because that is what they are, to drown out the noise of the gun-fire by running loud machinery. When they ran out of ammunition for the executions they obtained more ammunition to kill the rest of the evacuees from the supply element of OG South. And so JNA OG South provided not only the executioners but also the ammunition, logically and sensibly, to the executioners knowing that it would be used and for what purpose it would be used. Throughout the massacre local Serb TO, including the volunteers, remained subordinated to OG South. All units remained so until at 21st of November. Eventually, the order for resubordination of the TO occurred but only after the killing. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn to tab 3, and this is what I will call the resubordination on the 21st. Would you be kind enough, please, now to turn to tab 3, and this is what I will call the resubordination on the 21st. We can see that it is top left-hand corner, OG South command. The time is important. It's 6.00 a.m. in my language, and most others, 21st of November, 1991, after the killings had occurred. "Regulating the issue of resubordination and the return to home units ..." We can see the other highlighted area. In the course of the 21st of November, there is a suggestion about withdrawing the Leva Supoderica volunteers, the detachment and dispatch them, resubordinate them to another unit. If we look at paragraph 4: "The Vukovar TO units to be resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade, and continue with the carrying out the assign tasks ..." and we can see what the assigned tasks are, those related to Vojnovic and Vujanovic. If we turn the page, please, and we can see, it's not really highlighted but it's actually signed by Mrksic, although I think it's correct to say it was signed by Lieutenant Colonel Panic, his assistant, but the important point is clearly the time when the resubordination occurred. So we submit that the relevance is that it makes it clear that the resubordination takes effect at the earliest at 6.00 in the morning. It's submitted that the various units named all took part in the massacre at Ovcara and they were subordinated to OG South at all the relevant times. At least 200 non-Serbs from the Vukovar Hospital were executed at Ovcara. The bodies, as I say, of an additional 64 individuals who were removed still have not been found, and it's our submission that these missing individuals were also killed at Ovcara on the same night by the same Serb forces. Those 200 bodies were exhumed from a mass grave, and may I just deal, please, in summary, with what the findings were. Because there were 198 men and two women, we submit that is significant. The ages were from 17 years to 66. 55 per cent, which is over a hundred of them, of those examined had evidence of having received medical attention in the form of apparel or evidence of recent medical therapeutics. Gun-shot wounds caused the death in 195 of the individuals, and then there's reference to about sharp force. The manner of death of all the violent cases is homicide. And we submit the fact that they were male, their age, the percentage of people who were undergoing medical treatment and showed that they had been undergoing medical treatment demonstrates quite clearly that this evacuation agreement was a worthless piece of paper as far as the JNA and these three defendants were concerned. Early in the morning after the massacre, Captain Radic, Vujanovic and others were present at Radic's command post at Vujanovic's house in Vukovar where the massacre at Ovcara was actually discussed. One witness overheard that Major Sljivancanin had participated in the executions. The following day, there were rumours and discussions amongst the local population of Vukovar that something bad had happened at Ovcara. And as I say, a number of the executioners are members of the local TO. We submit that these defendants used Serb forces under their command to perform essential functions in the commission of the crimes. They acted in coordination amongst themselves and with other co-perpetrators, including Vujovic and Vujanovic. Mrksic, Sljivancanin, commanded or directed the Serb force under their command in various ways to evacuate the Croats and other non-Serbs, to guard and contain the detainees at the JNA barracks, to transfer the detainees to Ovcara farm and earlier, and clearly to mistreat and kill the detainees at Ovcara. Radic, we submit, personally and through the Serb forces under his command participated in the removal and the selection of Croats and other non-Serbs from Vukovar Hospital early in the hours of the 20th of November. Radic was the commander of the Serb forces who mistreated and killed the detainees at Ovcara. In addition, a number of people comprised of these defendants and other known and unknown individuals, those of which I have already nominated, had a common plan to persecute and kill the Croats and other non-Serbs taken from Vukovar Hospital by OG South and other Serb forces under the command of Colonel Mrksic to the Ovcara farm on the 20th. The common plan included all the crimes charged in the indictment. At minimum, the command plan included the crime of persecution, the rest of the crimes being foreseeable in the sense that they were likely consequences of the implementation of that common plan. These three accused did not physically commit any of the crimes charged in the indictment, but nonetheless contributed to the implementation of the common plan. With regard to 7(3), liability, clearly we must establish there existed a superior/subordinate relationship between the accused and the perpetrators of the offence, that the accused knew or had reason to know that the perpetrators were about to commit the offence or indeed had done so or that the accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the offence or to punish the perpetrators. The applicable test for whether the accused had superior responsibility for acts of the perpetrator clearly and on a common-sense basis has to be one of effective control. A superior had and has effective control over the perpetrator if at the time of the crimes charged in the indictment occurred he had the power to prevent their commission or to punish the perpetrators. We submit at all times relevant Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin had effective control over their subordinates. And finally, we submit at all times relevant to the indictment there existed a formal and well-organised system of military discipline and justice within the armed forces, JNA and TO. Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin availed themselves of none of the measures that were within their power at that time to prevent their subordinates from committing crimes or punishing them after learning of the crimes that had been committed, including an obligation to report such crimes as is stipulated by the armed force doctrine. We submit that these three men are guilty of these offences, and with the Court's leave we would seek to call evidence in due course in support of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Could I ask Mr. Vasic whether it is your intention to make an opening statement at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to inform you that the Defence of Mr. Mrksic does not intend to give an opening statement at this time, but we will do it at the start of our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Miroslav Radic shares the position of Mr. Vasic, or the Defence of Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence will give its opening statement before the opening of its case. But Mr. Sljivancanin informed me that he would like to use his right in accordance with Article -- Rule 84 bis and give a statement. He informed me that this would take about 20 minutes to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I be sure that neither your client, Mr. Vasic, nor your client, Mr. Borovic, wish to make a personal statement at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my client does not wish to address the Court at this time under the Rule mentioned by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Miroslav Radic decided to give a very brief statement that will not take more than two or three minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Mr. Borovic, we would call now upon Mr. Radic to make the brief statement that he indicates he would like to make at this time. Mr. Radic, you can stay seated or stand as you wish and speak from where you are. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED RADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving meet opportunity to speak. I will speak briefly, and I would like to state the following: First of all, would I like to say that it is very difficult to bear the burden of being accused for war crimes for which I personally believe that I'm innocent. I would also like to ask the Honourable Court at this time that during the proceedings they should establish the actual factual state of affairs and make it possible for the truth to be found and to be discovered. I hope that this institution will be a forum of truth and justice. I also hope that at the end of this trial justice will be satisfied and that all those guilty for the ill deeds that happened in the area of Vukovar would be punished for their deeds, the deeds which took place in 1992. This is all I wish to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Now, Mr. Lukic, we would call upon your client, Mr. Sljivancanin, who wishes to speak for a little longer time, we believe. Yes, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, my decision to address you in person through this statement is motivated by the desire to inform you of the frameworks of my truth in the firm belief that the truth, at the end of this trial, as I see it will be the truth that you -- as you will see it. This framework started when I took the solemn declaration when I joined the military academy. I have to read out the following: I, Veselin Sljivancanin, do solemnly declare to faithfully serve my people, to defend my homeland, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and to safeguard and defend the brotherhood and unity of our nations and the reputation of the Yugoslav People's Army, and that I will conscientiously obey the orders of my superiors. I will always be ready to fight for freedom and the honour of my homeland, and if need be, to lay down my life for it." I joined the army when I was 15 years old. I took the pledge to do my soldier's duty honourably and to defend my country which stretched as the lyrics of the song had it do, from Vagda River [phoen] to Mount Viglav [phoen], from Macedonia to Slovenija. That was my pledge, and I was always ready to lay down my life for it. Treachery, cowardice and dishonourable acts are concepts which neither I nor my ancestors ever experienced. They are a fate worse than death because in the land from which I come from, shame is inherited and passed down to future generations that are not responsible for what was done before them. In the Serb language, the word "moral" is derived from the word "must" in the sense of the internal obligation to behave honourably and decently, and in the part of the country that I come from this has a very literal meaning. That kind of attitude towards life is one that I passed down to the soldiers who were under my command, and they were soldiers of different ethnicities and religions. This is the second time that I have appeared in court. I appeared in court for the first time in 1998 in Belgrade and once again here and now. For a full 14 years, I was exposed to ugly lies and untruths, brutal propaganda, the loss of freedom and deprivation of many human rights. This propaganda appeared in the public information media depending on which political party or which politician needed to disseminate such propaganda on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. They ascribed much to me in that propaganda. They called me many things. I have been called a Chetnik, a dirty communist, a criminal, and a hero. The army in which I was a member was proclaimed an aggressor army, a Serbo-Chetnik army. The worst and most blatant untruth that was bandied about was that I hated the Croatian people. I and the soldiers of my army in Vukovar were those who helped the Croatian people most. Through military school and serving in the army, I was constantly there together with other members of other different ethnic groups living in Yugoslavia, and I never had any problems with any of them, least of all with the Croats. They are a Christian people, and I never felt any difference between us. In military schools, we -- they did not teach us to hate our own people, nor did we think that our army would ever have to fight against secessionists from within our own ranks. We were not taught to conquer other people's territory either or to jeopardise human freedoms. At the time, I was not aware of any republican borders. For me, all that existed was a single state, and that state's name was Yugoslavia, the most beautiful, most humane and freest country in the world at the time. Had Croatia been independent, neither I myself nor the soldiers within my unit would never have gone to Vukovar in the first place. I performed very responsible tasks always with the same objectivity, devotion, and self-sacrifice. When I completed the military academy, I was among the five best officers and selected to work in Tito's Guards. Until the end of Tito's life, I worked as a security detail for him and later as a security detail for other top ranking officials of Yugoslavia, including Franjo Tudjman when he came to attend meetings with the minister of the army, Kadijevic. I also provided security for many statesmen who visited my country. Amongst them I shall mention just a few: Jimmy Carter, Margaret Thatcher, Brezhnev, Mitterrand, Willy Brandt, Fidel Castro, Patini [phoen], Bush, Sr., Umadjen [phoen] and many others. And do I really look like a criminal to those who wrote the indictment, or perhaps they don't like the fact that I told Mr. Borsinger in 1991 in Vukovar in front of TV cameras the following, and I quote: "If you're not interested in the fact that my young soldiers are dying, soldiers who are 18 years old, 19 and 20 years old, then you are not a welcome man here." Mr. Borsinger, with a delegation of the International Red Cross, arrived on the 21st of November in the afternoon. He came to see me in the village of Negoslavci and apologised for the misunderstanding which took place one day before on the bridge on the Vuka River. I invite him to come to this Honourable Court and to tell the truth here. All of us officers and soldiers took the official declaration, the oath under the flag of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia pledging to safeguard that same country. When we were given the assignment to liberate the military garrison of the official country which was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Vukovar from the blockade and destruction which had been taken over by the secessionists who had already committed many crimes, the Yugoslav People's Army, which was the sole constitutional army arrived to perform its duty. You will judge, Your Honours, whether I should have indeed was obliged to act according to the law and the constitution and the pledge I had taken or whether I was supposed to trample on my obligations to trample on the constitution and the declaration I had made. If the situation were to repeat itself again, I would act in the same way as I did then. I am a soldier. I am not a politician, nor am I a lawyer. At school I was taught to respect the law and to carry out the orders of my superiors. Had I acted in any other way at that time that would have meant that I would have committed a crime against the armed forces and that I would have been a traitor and an immoral man. I have never violated the law or moral dictates. The irony of it is that there were people who had also taken the solemn declaration, just like me, under the same flag and under the same constitution. However, they went to join the other side, and they led a secessionist army, kill the people and the soldiers of the official army. I am very sorry about the families of all of the innocent people killed in Vukovar as well as in the territories of the former Yugoslavia. No one, not even this Court, can make up to a mother for the loss of her son, to a sister the loss of her brother, the wife the loss of her husband. All the victims have to be remembered, though. Each victim had their first and last name. I would like to and I must mention the names of some from whose fate everyone is turning their head, and they had their own truth and their own fate, and that truth must help you, Your Honours, to establish the complete truth. There can only be one truth. The first victims from the Guards Brigade in Vukovar were soldiers Damir Pinter, born in Zagreb; Ante Mrkonjic, from Tuzla; Darko Haluzan, from Celje; and Slobodan Paunovic from Surcin. They were killed while they were setting up tents where food was supposed to be prepared for their comrades. Nebojsa Zivancevic, an only child, Zoran Feldezdi, Zoran Elez, Goran Krstic, and Zeljko Popovic set off to the barracks on the 2nd of October. They missed the entrance, were captured by the secessionists and killed. Unfortunately, their bodies were found in the street of Sremskih Boraca on November 16th, 1991. They were burned. Lieutenant Vostic was running across the street in order to go and see his soldiers who were securing the barracks and he was killed. Second Lieutenant Borko Nikitovic went to visit his soldiers who were securing the barracks. He was hit by a sniper. Captain Sasa Milanovic tried to help him. He was killed in the back by a sniper. Major Velja Stojkovic and Lieutenant Vasilic were de-mining the mines laid down by terrorists, and they were hit by a mortar shell. Slobodan Popovic, an only child, my driver, was killed only because he happened to be driving a military vehicle. And there were many other such innocent victims. They all had a first and last name. They belonged to all ethnic groups but they were all members of one army. I mention these people because I knew them personally, because they were honourable and decent people, and I know that they never did anything bad to anyone. My driver just had a pistol and he never even tried to use it. Your Honours, I do not want to use these facts to draw attention away from the innocent who were killed, the people from the Vukovar Hospital. Those who did commit that crime should meet their just punishment. However, if this Court would like to establish the full truth about the Vukovar tragedy, they must learn all of the facts, each tragic human fate regardless of the name of the victim. Will this Court wish to know what Mile Dedakovic, called Jastreb, former JNA lieutenant colonel, was doing, a person who trampled the constitution, the laws, the flag, and the oath? His men put out a white flag on their vehicle, and then from that same vehicle bearing a white flag killed members of the regular army from automatic weapons. Many times I called him over the radio station in Vukovar in order to cease hostilities, to stop innocent people from getting killed and to stop the destruction of such a beautiful city. He refused all of that, and there is footage of that. When defeat was certain, Jastreb promised me, quote/unquote, that his Ustasha will find me wherever I happen to be, that I could not escape and that they would kill me. But he actually deserted from Vukovar just as he deserted from the JNA. Nobody of the Prosecutors, including the ones here, never even thought whether he and those like him should actually find themselves where I am now. Although I am not a lawyer, I believe that law and justice cannot find themselves on the wrong side of common sense. I believe that you will be convinced through documents which will be submitted by my Defence and through testimony of honourable witnesses that I have nothing to do with the crimes committed at Ovcara. I believe that this Trial Chamber will reject the statements of those Prosecution witnesses that are based on untruth, who only saw me in the public information media as well as of those witnesses who are using untruths in order to conceal their own irresponsible actions or who have gained something for themselves in return for agreeing to testify. I expect that honourable witnesses will appear here who will testify truthfully and tell you and the public what happened on the 20th of November, 1991. There is a great deal of irresponsibility in condemning an innocent person, and it is an even greater injustice when one who has contributed to the crime testifies in order to condemn an innocent person. Your Honours, I believe that it will be proved ultimately that the crimes at Ovcara were planned and committed by those who hated the JNA in order to sully its reputation and thwart its attempts to preserve Yugoslavia, and with the specific aim of discrediting and belittling us officers who loved our country. I am convinced that after all these years of persecution, all kinds of untruths and agony, I will finally receive justice. I want to believe that all the lies will finally be revealed and that truth will finally be heard. I hope that this Trial Chamber will accept only the law and reject non-law and acquit me of the charges ascribed to me without any valid proof. However, I already feel condemned after all this time in prison and after all the injustices and suffering my family, my friends, and I have been through. One thing sometimes that justice and righteousness unfortunately have not made any real gains in life since their foundations were laid two and a half millenia ago. Today, just like then, there is very little justice. It seems unattainable. However, honourable people do not give up on the path to justice. I am not asking for mercy, Your Honours. I expect to receive the truth and justice. Regardless of everything, I expect Your Honours to be just because when I am concerned, justice and the truth have the same weight, and I have faith that there is justice and that I will finally see it. This faith is based on the fact that in the conduct of my military duties and in life I never did anything dishonourable and that I always behaved properly towards all people, and that is why at the end I would like to quote the words of our literature Nobel laureate Ivo Andric. I quote: "There was not much justice in the world but the less there is of it the more it is worth. And yes, it is slow and want to come late but it does come sooner or later. That is why I always say rely on justice and do not be afraid." Gentlemen, I am not afraid. Those who committed injustice should be afraid as well as many others, because many are in danger if even one person is exposed to even a single injustice. Your Honours, I believe that at the end of this trial you will reach a decision that must be based on the full truth. In a just trial, which I expect, I am sure that my truth will ultimately become yours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sljivancanin. The proceedings today have proceeded --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The proceedings today have proceeded more quickly than had been anticipated, so that it will not be necessary for the Chamber to sit this afternoon or tomorrow as had been planned. A date has been set for the commencement of the hearing of the evidence, and that is on -- in two weeks' time, Tuesday the 25th of October. The hearing will now adjourn until then when the hearing of the evidence will continue. The Chamber will now adjourn until the 25th of October.
